newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Products Outlook - Demand keeps bears at bay.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Products Outlook - Demand keeps bears at bay.

text.p: Solid demand should keep record U.S. refinery runs in check amid signs the summer driving season underway since late May is delivering on its promise to put more motorists on the road, traders said.

To be sure, the underlying NYMEX basis slid hard last week and remained soft early Monday after the release of industry data showing U.S. refineries were pretty much running at full hilt, but demand for now should absorb much of that production and hold cash differentials in place.
"I think differentials will hold their ground because of demand and a variety of other factors," said one trader.
U.S. GULF COAST
In Gulf Coast markets, good demand may be complemented by unconfirmed talk that certain refiners in the region may be experiencing slight processing difficulties, traders said.

According to traders, who themselves are guessing who might be suffering from hiccups, the problems are with secondary units and are therefore not showing up in industry data that solely tracks primary input to distillation units.
"Things are going to be a bit stronger in the Gulf," said another trader, noting that tightness in Houston has to be getting a helping hand from refinery problems.

Feedstock traders in the region corroborated the talk, saying prices of vacuum gas oil, used in gasoline-producing catalytic cracking units, have been terribly soft lately amid a buildup of supplies suggestive of cat cracker problems.
On a more mundane level, the current prompt cycle for "M1" grade regular conventional gasoline will have a deadline for scheduling shipments in the Houston-to-New York Colonial Pipeline on Wednesday.

Scheduling deadlines on M1, easily the most liquid refined product market east of the Rocky Mountains, typically provide clues into the tone of the market. Refiners either flock to schedule causing differentials to firm, or they are nowhere to be seen and differentials turn soggy.
NEW YORK HARBOR
New York Harbor markets were looking mostly balanced, with the fate of prices pegged to gasoline import volumes, which, for the moment, appeared likely to diminish.

Cargo traders said the arbitrage window was closed early Monday by about $5-$6 a tonne, or 1.50 cents a gallon. Some predicted the second half of June would feature gasoline imports in a neutral zone of about 450,000 barrels per day, with the NYMEX selloff helping to put the cap in place. NYMEX July unleaded traded as far down as 56.50 cents a gallon Monday morning, off 0.63 cent from Friday's close, and 11.10 cents off of a recent high of 67.60 on May 23.
Another potentionally bearish factor is the delivery in New York Harbor of NYMEX gasoline that BP America took last week, though traders were mixed on that.
While some traders are not yet prepared to write off the bearish trend, others say prices cannot go much farther down given the demand pull from motorists hitting the roads.

"There's been a lot of pressure from the refinery output," one broker said, citing the Department of Energy's (DOE) data showing a record refinery utilization rate of 100.4 percent of capacity in last week's report.

"But I think the damage is done. In order to sustain the downtrend we would have to see (bearish demand statistics)," he said, noting this week's data from the DOE and the American Petroleum Institute (API) will be highly anticipated.
MIDCONTINENT
Midcontinent traders were meanwhile expecting cash gasoline differentials to slip by about a half cent toward the end of this week.
Supply in both the Group Three and Chicago markets have been flush given the record refinery run rates and demand that is weaker than in the other centers.
Higher shipments up the Colonial pipeline into Group Three have also been reported, which will add to supply.

"There is no shortage of supply," said a Group Three trader. "The retail price of gasoline is also a bit inflated so I think that will make some end users back off and think twice about taking a long weekend."
On Monday, Group Three unleaded differentials were about 5.00 cents to 5.25 cents over July NYMEX unleaded. Chicago was steady at 3.50/3.75 cents.
-- New York Oil Desk, 1 212 859 1620
